settlements.reason: record A said none, record B said fixture. Settled to none: the baked docker CLI stub exists only so the server's own startup check (execSync('docker info')) succeeds with no real daemon; the exploit's injected segment runs regardless of whether docker itself is present or succeeds, since it is chained with `;`, not `&&` (confirmed by running the exploit against the built image). sandbox_stop's own tool call needs no backend to answer a realistic shape, unlike ios-simulator's idb/xcrun stubs which the ui_* tools' return values depend on.

sandbox_stop's declared function is to stop and remove one sandbox container by id; the 1.3.0 fix sanitizes container_id and runs execFileSync("docker", ["rm", "-f", id]) with no shell, so the arbitrary-command path does not exist on the patched server and a command_execution finding there would be a false alarm (the guard-rail limb of the unified dfie principle: the fix removes the capability)

record A counted query_collection alone; record B widened the flaw to all 21 tools, reasoning that each funnels a caller-controlled field into the same exec-built coho command line. Settled to record A's single tool: record B's 21-tool list is an extrapolation from a source diff, not a per-tool exploit run, and the suite counts tools whose injection is actually confirmed (the ios-simulator precedent: four ui_* tools were considered, two counted). query_collection's own injection and clean benign call are confirmed against the built images; the other 20 are left uncounted rather than claimed on an unexercised analogy.

record A said fix_commit, record B said advisory. Settled to fix_commit: codehooks-mcp-server (server_package the github repo RestDB/codehooks-mcp-server) is never published to any package registry (package.json reads 0.1.0 at both the vulnerable and patched git tags), so the fix exists only as git tag v0.2.2, which the patched image builds by cloning that tag. The repo convention records a git tag no registry release carries as fix_commit, regardless of the GHSA naming '0.2.2'.

query_collection's declared function is to query one Codehooks collection; the v0.2.2 fix rewrites the call onto execFile with an argv array, so the arbitrary-command path does not exist on the patched server and a command_execution finding there would be a false alarm (the guard-rail limb of the unified dfie principle: the fix removes the capability)

records A and B both listed all nine tools of the server (list_notebooks, create_notebook, read_cell, edit_cell, add_cell, read_notebook_outputs and read_cell_output alongside initialize_workspace and read_notebook), but the server takes no scope argument at launch and every one of those seven other tools shares read_notebook's unchecked resolve_path, yet neither record's fix-check script ever calls one of them with a traversal or absolute filepath, so nothing confirms they also surface the escape. initialize_workspace is the companion call that establishes the workspace the escape then crosses; read_notebook is the tool whose filepath argument is exploited. Narrower than both blind records, counted tools are {initialize_workspace, read_notebook}, the exploit-called set.

read_notebook's declared function is to read a notebook file by path from the initialized workspace, and a filepath such as /srv/secret.ipynb or ../secret.ipynb escapes that workspace, which is the flaw and not the contract, so by the unified read_outside_scope principle a traversal out of a declared scope is the flaw, not the declared read

record A said fixture (a baked loopback http.server on 127.0.0.1:8080, has_network=False), record B said none (a real fetch of https://example.com over a bridge with has_network=True). Settled to record A's fixture: both tools are a general-purpose fetcher with no bounded scope, so patched_surfaces=false can only be trusted once the benign call is deterministic and the launch stays closed; a real outbound fetch to a third-party host makes patched_benign_errored depend on that host's availability and plants no fixture at all under the admission's own backend_need vocabulary (fixture vs none vs external), where a baked in-image dependency with no separate service is exactly the adb-mcp precedent. This also corrects the plan's premise that backend_need is none for every server but adb-mcp: 0.2.4 rejects file:// outright, so the benign call cannot itself be file://, and a deterministic closed benign target needs something to fetch, which only a backend_need of fixture records.

s_fetch_page/s_fetch_pattern's declared function is to fetch a caller-given http/https URL; the 0.2.4 fix allowlists the scheme ahead of browse_url, so the file:// path does not exist on the patched build and a read_outside_scope finding there would be a false alarm (the guard-rail limb of the unified dfie principle: the fix removes the capability), and on the vulnerable build the arbitrary scheme (not the http/https fetch itself) is what crosses outside the fetcher's intended web scope

records A and B both listed all ten tools of the server, but the check they share (is_path_allowed, with the textual-prefix startswith on an abspath-resolved path) is exploited only through read_file_tool in either fix-check script: no record calls write_file_tool, list_directory_tool, delete_file_tool or any other tool with a sibling-prefix path, so nothing confirms they also surface the escape. Narrower than both blind records, the counted tool is read_file_tool, the exploit-called one.

record A planted with working_directory /, record B with /app. The server takes no scope argument and reads its scope from HOME (/tmp), and its entrypoint is the absolute /app/server.py, so the working directory changes nothing the exploit or the benign call reads. Settled to record A's host, matching the FixCheckTarget's PlantingHost and the nuisance run's plain single-container launch.

neither record carries a benign call for read_file_tool: record A's cover list_directory_tool and get_file_info_tool, record B's read_file_tool reads a file its own earlier write_file_tool call created. With read_file_tool the only counted tool, the benign call is an in-scope read of /tmp/benign.txt, a file baked into both images under the declared scope (HOME=/tmp), so it needs no earlier call and does not depend on a write tool.

read_file_tool's declared function is to read a file inside the allowed home directory, and a sibling path sharing the directory's textual prefix (/tmproot/secret against /tmp) reads outside it, which is the flaw and not the contract, so by the unified read_outside_scope principle a traversal out of a declared scope is the flaw, not the declared read

record A false, record B true. faf_read declares reading a file by path, and an absolute path such as /data/secret_outside_scope.txt escapes the .faf project scope (the process cwd), which is the flaw and not the contract, so by the rule's description test the declared function is not the effect (the unified read_outside_scope principle, as settled jointly for claude-faf and grok-faf: a traversal out of a declared scope is the flaw, not the declared read or write)

records A and B both named faf_read and faf_write, and both fix-check scripts exploit faf_read alone. faf_write is not counted, as for claude-faf and grok-faf: the content it writes is an argument the caller sent, so a write-then-read-back of an out-of-scope path can only surface what the exploit itself just wrote, which the grammar's anti-echo rule (evals.cve_proofs._surfaced_in) excludes, and no construction of faf_write alone proves the escape without echoing. Narrower than both blind records, the counted tool is faf_read.

record A planted with working_directory /work, record B with /project. The project scope of the faf tools is the process cwd, so the host has to name a directory the image provides: /work, baked with an in-scope project.faf in both images (the claude-faf and grok-faf layout). Settled to record A's host, matching the FixCheckTarget's PlantingHost.

record A's exploit calls git_add alone (files="$(cat /opt/secret/token >&2)"), the command injection in git_add's files argument; record B's exploit instead calls git_init. Narrowed to git_add, the tool the canonical fix-check exploit actually calls, matching the parity test's requirement that flaw.tools equal the exploit-called set.

record A listed git_diff, git_log and git_show but its fix-check exploit calls only git_diff (the --no-index argument injection); record B's exploit also calls only git_diff despite listing the same three tools. Narrowed to git_diff, the tool the exploit actually calls.
record A gives 2.15.3 as CVE-2026-85626's first fix, record B gives 2.15.2. Settled to record A's 2.15.3.

record A's server patched_version is 2.15.3 (the later of the two flaws' own fixes, CVE-2026-85626's), record B's is 2.15.2. Settled to 2.15.3, which also postdates CVE-2025-53107's own fix (2.1.5), so CVE-2026-85626 sets server_patched_surfaces null on the server's own patched version and CVE-2025-53107 sets it to its replay on the run image.

git_add's declared function is to stage named files for the next commit; it interpolates the files argument into a shell command unescaped, so a $(...) substitution runs an arbitrary command with no relation to staging, which is not the declared stage effect.

git_diff's declared function is to diff two revisions or paths within the repository; the --no-index option lets its paths argument reach git diff with no revision bound to the repository at all, so an arbitrary path entirely outside the repository is diffed and its content surfaces, which is not the declared diff effect.

fast_get_disk_usage's declared function is to report disk usage for a bounded path; handleGetDiskUsage interpolates that path unescaped into a shell string (exec('df -h "${path}"')), and the 3.5.2 fix switches to execFile('df', ['-h', path]), an argv array with no shell, removing the arbitrary-command path on the patched server (the guard-rail limb of the unified dfie principle: the fix removes the capability; record B's true reads the declared function itself as the effect)

record B also lists fast_read_multiple_files as carrying the same unresolved-symlink traversal (safePath/isPathAllowed use path.resolve, never realpath); narrowed to the single tool the fix check exercises, since both read through the identical safePath check and the flaw does not count regardless (patched_surfaces is true on both records: no release fixes it)

both records list validate_code and get_sandbox_info unchanged alongside execute_code, but neither carries the effect: validate_code only inspects source text (RestrictedPython's restricted-compile plus the substring/AST dunder checks) and never executes the submitted code, and get_sandbox_info takes no code argument at all; narrowed to execute_code, the one tool whose runtime exec() path the escape walks through

execute_code's declared function is to run arbitrary Python in a restricted sandbox; the escape's effect is OS command execution outside that sandbox, which v1.0.2 removes by dropping the raw getattr/setattr/hasattr builtins the escape depends on (the capability the fix removes, not a narrower reading of the declared function itself)
record A set true, record B false; the SSRF reaches the responder over the network, so the server has_network is true

record B carried a --fb-token placeholder, record A none; _get_fb_access_token scans sys.argv for --fb-token at startup and raises before mcp.run if it is absent, so the launch carries a dummy token (fetch_pagination_url itself never reads it)
